title: They require indifference and indetermination: the common description of freedom
source_text: XLI. Nec enim volunt libertatem esse sine quadam agentis liberi ad agendum indifferentia & indeterminatione; & eos solos actus liberos esse putant quorum contrarium facere possumus, aut saltem eos omittere, & ab iis cessare: juxta vulgarem illam libertatis descriptionem, per quam in eo consistere dicitur quod agens liberum positis omnibus ad agendum praerequisitis possit agere, vel non agere, hoc, aut illud agere.
pass_a_gloss: For they will not have liberty to be without a certain indifference and indetermination of the free agent to acting; and they think those acts alone free whose contrary we can do, or at least omit them, and cease from them: according to that common description of liberty, by which it is said to consist in this, that the free agent, all prerequisites for acting being posited, can act, or not act, do this, or that.
pass_b_english: They do not allow freedom without some indifference and indeterminacy in the free agent with respect to acting. Only those acts are free, they think, whose opposite we can do, or which we can at least leave undone and break off.
This follows the familiar description of freedom, which places it in this: given everything required beforehand for acting, the free agent can act or not act, and can do this or that.

lemmas.gloss: all prerequisites for acting being posited

choices.why: Kept as in the preceding locus on free choice in general, so the Roman and Reformed accounts are compared in one vocabulary.
